title: Toxicity of fluorescent silica nanoparticles in brine shrimp and their implications as food ingestion markers.

sections.heading: Materials and methods

operations.sentence: For rearing adult shrimp, nauplii (shrimp larvae) were transferred into an 8 L tank and raised in filtered natural seawater (3% salinity) at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) under a 12/12 h illumination cycle.

Effects on the feeding rate Nauplii, 18–24 h after hatching, were transferred into glass vials (50 nauplii per vial) containing 10 mL of a suspension mixture of dead baker’s yeast (~ 2 × 10 5  cells/mL, heat-killed at 70 °C for 5 min) with or without 16 mg/L FSNPs.

Nauplii, 18–24 h after hatching, were dark-incubated in a suspension mixture of 16 mg/L FSNPs and 1 × 10 6  cells/mL of baker’s yeast for 1 h. Then, the nauplii were washed with seawater and passed through a 110 μm net.
A control group was maintained in artificial seawater without FSNPs.

The FSNP suspension was then added to each well to reach a final NP concentration of 16 mg/L. Observations were made every 5 min under UV light to detect the appearance of abdominal fluorescence, followed by further monitoring until luminescent feces were detected, indicating complete gut passage of the ingested FSNPs.

Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-11858-2.

Introduction One major challenge in observing the feeding behavior of zooplankton, especially at the individual level, stems from their minuscule body size. A conventional method used so far to study zooplankton feeding is measuring the remaining food over a certain period after providing a known amount 1 – 3 . The quantity of food consumed was calculated based on the final concentration of residual algal cells after feeding or the amount of carbon or pigments as a proxy for food. The primary results are generally the characteristics of the whole population or sample group tested, and mathematical or statistical techniques are applied to infer those of individual plankton 2 , 3 . Food ingestion can be simply observed under a microscope by mounting plankton on a glass slide and their transparent bodies allowing for the observation of food particles traveling through the gut passage 4 , 5 . However, this method inevitably disturbs or harms the subject which might not reflect its normal behavior. More advanced approaches have been developed, in which the test animals must be fixed onto a needle or holder, which allows their behavior to be observed either from a video recorded via a macro lens or by electrochemical techniques 6 , 7 . It assesses not only the feeding activity at the individual level but also other physiological characteristics. However, it requires sophisticated apparatus and is not affordable. Nanotechnology is rapidly becoming a tool in many research areas, including aquatic science. For instance, researchers can track the movement trajectories of small zooplankton employing quantum dots (QDs), a fluorescent semiconductor nanocrystal, as well as apply image processing and tracking softwares 8 , 9 . The surface of the QDs is modified for adherence to the plankton body, and the tagged plankton can be located under ultraviolet (UV) light. However, the QDs have not been used to observe feeding activity. Alternatively, in several studies, test animals have been allowed to ingest micro or nanoscale fluorescent plastic beads, enabling tracking through their digestive tracts 10 – 12 . However, their potential toxicity limits their use, as these studies often focus on ecotoxicity rather than feeding behavior tracking. Fluorescent silica nanoparticles (FSNPs) are nanosized silica particles that incorporate fluorescent dye molecules within their matrix. They present a promising alternative for observing the feeding behavior of zooplankton owing to their excellent fluorescence brightness and photostability. This characteristic is attributed to the numerous dye molecules packed into a small area within the matrix, which protects the fluorophores from oxygen-induced fluorescence bleaching, thus prolonging their usability 13 , 14 . In addition, when used in vivo, FSNPs prevent direct contact between potentially harmful fluorophores and organisms 15 . The surface silanol groups (≡ Si-OH) also allow for easy modification, enabling cross-linking with biomolecules to act as biosensors, achieving specific targeting of certain cells or tissues 13 , 16 , 17 . One major concern when applying marking materials in live organisms is their potential toxicity. Silica nanoparticles (SNPs) in their crystalline form are highly toxic and thus are rarely used in biological applications, unlike amorphous silica, which is less toxic and more compatible with biological systems 18 . However, ambiguities remain regarding the toxicity of amorphous SNPs, even in the same test organisms 19 – 21 . Among aquatic organisms, the toxicity of SNPs against crustacean zooplankton has mostly been examined in the freshwater flea,  Daphnia magna , as a representative organism, with varied results 22 . However, their impacts on other species, especially marine zooplankton, have been reported infrequently. Several factors should be considered when selecting markers for applicability in small animals 23 . This study focused on four key aspects to evaluate the potential of FSNPs as markers for tracking feeding behavior in the brine shrimp ( Artemia franciscana ), which is a nonselective filter feeder, as a representative model for marine zooplankton. First, the FSNPs should be able to disperse well in the medium (seawater) to ensure that the target organisms can equally access them. Second, they must be nontoxic and do not interfere with normal behavior at their working concentration. Third, they must emit a distinct signal that is easily detectable. Finally, they must pass through the digestive tract simultaneously with the ingested food and be excreted along with the feces.

Results Physical characteristics of the FSNPs FSNPs were spherical with a diameter of 64.0 ± 3.9 nm ( n  = 90) (Fig.  1 a). At an excitation wavelength of 365 nm, the wavelength of the UV lamp used, their maximal emission wavelength was 614 nm when dispersed in distilled or seawater (Fig.  1 b). When the FSNPs were exposed to an excitation wavelength of 460 nm, which is the maximal excitation wavelength of the Rubpy dye incorporated in the NPs, the peak emission wavelengths were 614 and 617 nm for those dispersed in distilled and seawater, respectively. The average zeta potential of FSNPs in seawater (pH 8.2, conductivity 55.57 mS/cm) was − 59.69 ± 10.67 mV ( n  = 3), which falls within the range for good dispersion stability in the medium 24 . 
 Fig. 1 ( a ) A transmission electron microscope (TEM) image of FSNPs at 100,000× magnification and ( b ) emission spectra of the 100 mg/L FSNP suspension in distilled or seawater at excitation bands of 365 and 460 nm. 
 Acute toxicity No apparent sign of acute toxicity was detected in the brine shrimp nauplii treated with a range of FSNP concentrations for 24 h (Table  1 ), with no differences in mortality or immobility between the tested groups (mortality: χ 2  = 10.65, df = 11,  P  = 0.473; immobility: χ 2  = 9.03, df = 11,  P  = 0.619). However, after 48 h, the mortality varied significantly within the FSNP-treated groups (χ 2  = 22.99, df = 11,  P  = 0.018), but not when compared to the control. The immobility at 48 h did not differ markedly among all treatments (χ 2  = 13.33, df = 11,  P  = 0.273).

 Appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking Fluorescence due to FSNPs was observed at all tested concentrations. It was observed only in the gut, indicating that the FSNPs could not attach to other body parts (Fig.  2  and Supplementary Video 1). The marking efficiency was markedly enhanced with an increase in FSNP concentrations until 4 mg/L (Fig.  3 a). The presence of food did not affect the marking efficiency, but interacted with FSNPs (Table  2 ).

 The fluorescence brightness of the marked individuals was influenced by FSNP concentration and the presence of food (Table  2 ). The brightness score elevated with an increase in FSNP concentration until 16 mg/L; it was greater under the condition of food absence than presence (Fig.  3 b). Based on these findings, 16 mg/L FSNPs was identified as the optimal concentration (representing the lowest concentration that achieved high marking efficiency and fluorescence intensity) and was subsequently used in the following experiments. Effects on locomotion The average movement speeds of brine shrimp in the 16 mg/L FSNP suspension ( n  = 46) and those in the control ( n  = 42) were 3.20 ± 1.06 and 3.22 ± 1.10 mm/s, respectively, which were not significantly different between the treatments (W = 968.0,  P  = 0.990). Similarly, the average distances traveled in 30 s were 95.89 ± 31.92 and 96.44 ± 33.06 mm for the FSNP-treated and control groups, which were not markedly different (W = 968.0,  P  = 0.990). Feeding rate Feeding rates after correcting for the yeast autolysis rate (2.60 ± 4.26 × 10 3  cells/h) in the absence ( n  = 7) and presence ( n  = 7) of 16 mg/L FSNPs were 33.04 ± 47.98 and 34.03 ± 77.43 cells/h/individual, respectively, which were not markedly different between the two conditions (W = 21.5,  P  = 0.749). Persistence of FSNPs in brine shrimp After providing 16 mg/L FSNPs under food absence or presence, followed by depuration in artificial seawater, stereo microscopic observations indicated that the luminescence of FSNPs in the brine shrimp was bright only during the first 15 min of depuration as the gut of most individuals was still filled with FSNPs. However, after 15 min, most FSNPs were excreted from the gut, resulting in fainter luminescence in the digestive tract, and luminescent fecal pellets could be detected. Considering the number of brine shrimp with luminescence regardless of the intensity, the presence or absence of food resulted in a variation in FSNP clearance from the gut (Table  3 ). Under food absence, although most ingested FSNPs could be excreted from the gut within 15 min, a small number remained in the guts of most brine shrimp and persisted for > 24 h (Fig.  4 ). In contrast, no detectable FSNPs were observed in approximately 80% of the shrimp tested under food presence after 15 min of depuration. These results were also confirmed using a fluorescence microscope (Fig.  5 ). FSNPs did not adhere to any other part of the shrimp except for the digestive tract; observable FSNPs were not found in most shrimp after 15 min of depuration under food presence.

 Chronic toxicity In the chronic toxicity test conducted with 16 mg/mL FSNPs under different exposure conditions over 14 days, the lethal time 50 (LT 50 ) values for brine shrimp in the 3-hour intermittent exposure, 6-hour intermittent exposure, and continuous exposure groups were 12.8, 11.5, and 8.9 days, respectively. The LT 50  for the control group (artificial seawater without FSNPs) was not calculated, as 71% of brine shrimp remained alive at the end of the experiment. Significant differences in survival curves were observed among the treatment groups (χ² = 27.4, df = 3,  P  < 0.001; Fig.  7 ). Brine shrimp exposed to FSNPs under all treatment conditions exhibited shorter lifespan compared to the control group (Supplementary Table 1). When analyzing survival during the first 6 days of exposure, significant differences were also detected among the treatment groups (χ² = 13.0, df = 3,  P  = 0.005). However, only the continuous exposure group showed significantly lower survival compared to the control, while the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups did not differ significantly from the control during this initial period (Supplementary Table  1 ). 
 Fig. 7 Survival curves of brine shrimp exposed to FSNPs over a 14-day period under three exposure conditions: 3-hour exposure every 48 h, 6-hour exposure every 48 h, and continuous exposure. The control group was maintained in artificial seawater without FSNPs. Each treatment consisted of 9 replicates, with 10 brine shrimp per replicate. 
 Throughout the experiment, more than 70% of brine shrimp in the continuous exposure group exhibited fluorescence under UV light at each observation point (every 48 h). In contrast, in both the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups, fluorescence was detected within 30 min after FSNP administration but was no longer detectable after 48 h seawater renewal. Tests in adults Fluorescence due to ingested FSNPs can be seen in the abdomen of the adult shrimp (Fig.  8  and Supplementary Video  2 ), while their feces remained as small pellets at the bottom of the container. The average times that the shrimp abdomens began to fluoresce after FSNP exposure were 14.4 and 18.8 min for males ( n  = 25) and females ( n  = 21), respectively. However, they were not significantly different between the sexes (W = 285,  P  = 0.601). The average times that the fluorescent feces appeared due to the excretion of ingested FSNPs were similar between males and females (W = 275.5,  P  = 0.775), which were 38.2 and 39.0 min after providing FSNPs, respectively.

Discussion The application of FSNPs synthesized using the water-in-oil reverse microemulsion technique has been successful as an internal marker in fruit flies, demonstrating several benefits such as bright fluorescence, photostability, and low toxicity 15 . This study reports that these NPs were well-dispersed in seawater, as indicated by the zeta potentials. They exhibited low toxicity during short-term exposure and could be traced through the gut passage when ingested, detectable under a stereomicroscope, or even with the naked eye, suggesting their potential usefulness as markers for studying feeding behavior in marine zooplankton. Our study demonstrated that FSNPs exhibited nonacute toxicity to brine shrimp nauplii across all concentrations tested (1–1,024 mg/L), and the selected concentration (16 mg/L) had no effect on locomotion behavior. This result aligns with a previous study conducted on fruit flies with the same FSNPs 15 . The silica shell encasing the fluorophore molecules can prevent direct contact with animal tissues. Additionally, SNPs are generally less toxic and are sometimes considered compatible with biological systems 21 , 24 – 27 . However, their toxicity can vary significantly based on their characteristics and the intrinsic factors of the test organisms 22 . For example, a study 19  found that smaller NPs with surface silanol groups, which could potentially denature cell membrane proteins, were more toxic than larger or surface-modified NPs. Despite the SNPs synthesized via the water-in-oil reverse microemulsion technique having free silanol groups 28 , no apparent acute toxicity was observed in our tests. This result may be due to the protective cuticle of the brine shrimp, which could prevent the NPs from directly contacting the internal tissues. Further research is necessary to fully understand these interactions. Research on the susceptibility of microcrustaceans to SNPs has largely focused on the freshwater flea  D. magna , whose environmental conditions differ markedly from the high-salinity habitats of brine shrimp. Despite this, the reported toxicity in terms of LC 50  and EC 50  values ranged from 2 to > 10,000 mg/L 29 . To date, only a limited number of experiments have been conducted on brine shrimp with SNPs, with findings that indicated variable toxicities. The findings of Rekulapally et al. 26  and Tayemeh et al. 30  align with ours, indicating that SNPs at the maximum tested concentration of 100 mg/L were nontoxic at 24 h of exposure. Conversely, Gutner-Hoch et al. 31  reported moderate toxicity (LC 50  = 12.29 mg/L). As discussed earlier, these differences are likely attributable to variations in NP characteristics such as size, surface chemistry, and preparation techniques. This study used baker’s yeast as the food source for brine shrimp, rather than their natural diet of microalgae, to avoid confounding luminescence signals from the algal chlorophylls (664 and 647 nm for chlorophyll a and b, respectively), which have fluorescence peaks close to those of FSNPs (614–617 nm) 32 . Our results indicated that ingested food could reduce the fluorescence signal observed in the gut of brine shrimp. However, at the optimal concentration of 16 mg/L, the presence of food no longer had a significant effect on the signal of FSNPs (Fig.  3 b). It should be noted that a semi-quantitative scoring method in our study was performed to assess fluorescence brightness, as it allowed for a practical and efficient evaluation of a large number of individuals under a stereomicroscope. Additionally, all observations were conducted by the same examiner to minimize observer bias and ensure consistency. For more precise and quantitative assessments, imaging systems coupled with fluorescence intensity measurements and tracking software, as applied in previous studies 8 , 9 , could be utilized in future work. Regarding feeding rate, our findings indicated that FSNPs did not influence the shrimp feeding rate. However, it is important to note that yeast is not an ideal diet for brine shrimp because the rigid cell walls hinder digestion 33 . The feeding rates observed in our experiments were low because some yeast cells remained undigested and were excreted intact, as indicated by the fluorescence image (Fig.  6 b). Clogging and accumulation of small particles in the digestive tract are crucial factors to be considered when assessing the suitability of FSNPs as a feeding marker. Such NPs might block the gut passage and impede nutrient assimilation, resulting in abnormal feeding behavior and mortality, as reported previously 11 . Our results indicated that most brine shrimp could egest FSNPs within 15 min for nauplii and 40 min for adults, concurrently with the ingested food, as evidenced by the luminescent fecal pellets. This expulsion time was similar to previous findings, in which the time for ingested food to travel through the gut passage of brine shrimp was ~ 30 min, regardless of the body size 34 . However, under the food absence condition, the excretion of the NPs from their guts was difficult, and many individuals still retained the FSNPs for > 24 h after ingestion. Similar results have been reported before as the pressure from recently ingested food particles is required to expel the NPs 10 , 35 , 36 . Ingested FSNPs were expelled as pellets that sank to the bottom, both in the presence or absence of food. This observation contrasted with the well-dispersed state of FSNPs before ingestion. This phenomenon has been explained by the naturally produced chitinous membranes in the midgut to encase anything consumed, preventing the food from passing through the gut too quickly 35 . Adherence of different types of NPs to the surfaces or appendages of microcrustaceans has been observed, including nanoplastics 8 , 9 , 12 . This adherence has been attributed to the surface charges of both the NPs and the organisms 10 . For instance, the use of QDs to track the movements of water fleas required a modification of the NP surface to have a positive charge or coated with biotin, facilitating the biotinylation of the water flea cuticle 8 , 9 . In contrast, in our study, fluorescence microscopy observations revealed that FSNPs were localized exclusively in the digestive tracts of brine shrimp, without adherence to other body parts. The zeta potentials of FSNPs in seawater indicated a negative charge, mirroring that of the microcrustacean cuticle 8 . This same charge likely prevents the FSNPs from adhering to or penetrating the tissues of brine shrimp due to electrostatic repulsion. Brine shrimp are nonselective filter feeders that ingest particles, including food and even sand grains, < 50 μm 37 . Consequently, FSNPs can be ingested and accumulated in the gut. Although fluorescent micro and nanoplastics used have exhibited fluorescence in the gut, which was similar to the objective of our study, they are toxic to brine shrimp and have been used to test their negative effects from an environmental perspective rather than for feed tracking 10 , 12 . Our study demonstrated that a low concentration of FSNPs at 16 mg/L effectively allowed the observation of their feeding behavior—using a stereomicroscope for nauplii and with the naked eye for adults; it showed no adverse impacts on the brine shrimp in our investigations. Thus, we opted for this concentration to avoid the excessive use of FSNPs and to reduce the potential negative effects. By simultaneously providing DAPI-stained yeast and FSNPs as food, we confirmed that both co-travel during gut transit and are expelled with normal feces. However, we observed numerous blue dots along the gut wall, likely from DAPI molecules binding to the DNA in the nuclei of the epithelial cells. This finding suggests that conventional dye staining of food items may not be appropriate for tracking feeding behavior, as the dye can also stain the cells, potentially interfering with observations and posing a toxicity risk. Although no acute toxicity was observed, our additional chronic toxicity experiments indicated that continuous and repeated exposure to FSNPs at 16 mg/L induced significant mortality over time. LT 50  values of FSNPs from our study were similar to those previously reported for  A. salina , where LT 50  values of 18.8 and 17.9 days were observed following exposure to SNPs at concentrations of 5 and 10 mg/L, respectively 30 . Two possible mechanisms may account for this delayed toxicity. First, while FSNPs could be excreted from the digestive tract, continuous exposure resulted in their persistent presence in the gut, potentially causing blockage that impaired food digestion and assimilation, ultimately leading to starvation 11 . Second, toxic effects of FSNPs as discussed earlier may emerge with repeated or prolonged exposure 19 , 22 . This could explain the significant increase in mortality observed in the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups after 6 days, despite the absence of detectable accumulation following depuration. Although this study demonstrated the effects of FSNP exposure on brine shrimp through behavioral and survival assessments, it did not include biochemical or molecular biomarkers, which could provide deeper insights into the underlying mechanisms of toxicity. Previous studies have shown that exposure to NPs can alter enzymatic activities related to oxidative stress and detoxification pathways in  Artemia , including glutathione S-transferase (GST), catalase (CAT), and cholinesterase (ChE) 38 , 39 . For example, Gambardella et al. 39  reported that metal oxide NPs significantly altered GST and ChE activities, even in the absence of acute mortality, highlighting their importance in xenobiotic metabolism and neurotoxicity assessment. Similarly, Varó et al. 38  found that amino-modified polystyrene NPs induced oxidative stress and modulated gene expression related to development ( clap ), molting ( cstb ), stress response ( hsp70 ), and immunity ( proPO  and  lysozyme ) in  A. franciscana . Additionally, transcriptomic analyses have shown that exposure to SNPs can affect genes involved in stress response and cuticle renewal in aquatic invertebrates 40 . These findings suggest that prolonged FSNP exposure may plausibly affect cellular and molecular pathways in  Artemia , even in the absence of apparent acute toxicity. Therefore, future studies incorporating gene expression and enzymatic biomarkers would be valuable for confirming the mechanistic basis of FSNP-induced stress and toxicity.

Conclusions This study demonstrated that FSNPs present a promising tool for observing the feeding behavior of marine zooplankton. They showed excellent dispersion stability in seawater and exhibited low acute toxicity. Critically, they were effectively ingested and expelled by the brine shrimp, allowing for a clear observation of the feeding processes without adhering to the shrimp’s outer surfaces or causing significant adverse effects. Our findings indicate that FSNPs can be utilized to track the passage of ingested food through the gut, providing valuable insights into the feeding behavior of zooplankton. FSNPs at 16 mg/L were sufficient to mark the shrimp without affecting their locomotion during short time exposure. However, prolonged or repeated exposure negatively affected survival, indicating potential long-term risks. The presence of food facilitated the clearance of FSNPs from their digestive tract. Their ease of observation under UV light makes them particularly useful for such applications. Future research should investigate the molecular-level effects of FSNPs on zooplankton and assess their bioaccumulation and biomagnification potential in other marine species to evaluate their broader applicability in ecological studies.

Materials and methods Nanoparticle characterization FSNPs were synthesized according to the method outlined by Songvorawit, et al. 15  using the water-in-oil reverse microemulsion technique, and Rubpy dye (tris [2,2′-bipyridyl]ruthenium[II] chloride) as a fluorophore. The NPs were examined under a JEM-1400 transmission electron microscope (TEM; JEOL, Tokyo, Japan), and their size was measured from the TEM images employing the ImageJ software version 1.53o (NIH, USA;  https://imagej.nih.gov/ij ). Since this study used FSNPs suspended in saline water, their dispersion stability was examined in artificial seawater (ASTM D1141-98, pH 8.2) utilizing a Nano ZSP zeta-sizer (Malvern Panalytical, Great Malvern, England). Emission spectra were examined employing a Duetta ™  fluorometer (Horiba Scientific, Kyoto, Japan) at excitation bands of 365 and 460 nm, which corresponded to the UV light wavelength used to track animal behavior in this study and the maximal excitation wavelength of Rubpy dye, respectively 14 . The maximal emission wavelength of the FSNPs was calculated using a moving average based on five data points. Test animals and handling Commercial brine shrimp ( Artemia franciscana ) cysts (American Eagle, USA) imported from the Great Salt Lake, USA were purchased from a local supplier in Bangkok, Thailand. They were hatched in artificial seawater at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and illumination. For rearing adult shrimp, nauplii (shrimp larvae) were transferred into an 8 L tank and raised in filtered natural seawater (3% salinity) at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) under a 12/12 h illumination cycle. Artificial food (composition unknown, branded as N.P. Guppy, Thailand) purchased from a local seller in Bangkok, Thailand, was provided every other day, and the adults were obtained 3 weeks after hatching. Euthanasia was performed utilizing the two-step method (immersion in 5% ethanol for 5 min and then 10% formalin) per the AVMA guidelines 41 . The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University (Protocol Review No. 2423018). Acute toxicity test Nauplii, 18–24 h post-hatching, were transferred into 24-well plates containing 1–1,024 mg/L of FSNP suspension in artificial seawater (2 mL of suspension and 10–20 nauplii per well) and cultured at 25–26 °C under a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) with a 12/12 h light/dark cycle. Brine shrimp grown in artificial seawater without FSNPs were used as a control. Mortality and immobility were checked at 24 and 48 h after exposure. A nauplius was considered dead if its appendages stopped moving within 10 s. Immobility was identified when a nauplius remained with moving appendages in situ for 10 s and was calculated by dividing the number of immobile (but still alive) individuals by the total number of living individuals. A mortality rate in the 24-h period of less than 10% was considered valid for the control group. Each treatment was conducted in eight replications. Test for the appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking To ensure that all tested brine shrimp were ready to eat the food provided, 15–30 nauplii, 24–36 h after hatching were used. Chronic toxicity test Based on the results of the appropriate FSNP concentration experiment, a concentration of 16 mg/L FSNPs was used for the chronic toxicity test. Brine shrimp nauplii (18–24 h post-hatching) were transferred to 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 150 mL of artificial seawater under continuous aeration, with 10 nauplii per flask. They were fed with artificial food, and both seawater and food were renewed every 48 h. Three treatment groups were performed: (1) continuous exposure to FSNPs, (2) 3-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h, and (3) 6-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h. In treatments (2) and (3), nauplii were exposed to FSNPs prior to the renewal of seawater and food. The experiment was conducted over a period of 14 days. A control group was maintained in artificial seawater without FSNPs. Rearing conditions and mortality assessment criteria were consistent with those used in the acute toxicity test. Each treatment was conducted in nine replications. Test with adult brine shrimp Adult brine shrimp, 25 males and 24 females, were used to evaluate whether FSNPs could be applied to developed stages. The sexes were determined by the presence of a clasping organ (male) and brood sac (female). The shrimp were randomly selected from an aquarium and transferred into 24-well plates filled with 2 mL of baker’s yeast suspension (1 × 10 6  cells/mL), one individual per well. They were dark-acclimatized for 30 min. The FSNP suspension was then added to each well to reach a final NP concentration of 16 mg/L. Observations were made every 5 min under UV light to detect the appearance of abdominal fluorescence, followed by further monitoring until luminescent feces were detected, indicating complete gut passage of the ingested FSNPs. Statistical analyses Because our data did not meet the assumption for parametric statistics, nonparametric statistical analyses were used in all tests. The effects of FSNP concentration on mortality and immobility were ascertained by applying the Kruskal–Wallis test; Dunn’s test was used for pairwise comparison. The effects of FSNP concentration, the presence or absence of food, and their interaction with the marking efficiency or fluorescence brightness of the marked individuals were analyzed employing the aligned rank test. Feeding rates in the presence and absence of FSNPs were corrected for the rate of yeast autolysis in the control group and then compared by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The effects of depuration time, the presence or absence of food, and their interactions were analyzed using the aligned rank and Dunn’s tests. Locomotion data for shrimp treated with FSNPs were compared with the control utilizing the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The number of times that the abdomen of adult brine shrimp exhibited luminescence and the number of times that the fluorescent feces appeared due to the excretion of FSNPs were compared between sexes using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. LT 50  was analyzed using probit analysis in SPSS version 28.0 44 . All other statistical analyses were performed using the base, ARTool, combinate, dplyr, survival, survminer, and tidyverse packages in R, version 4.3.0 45 .

To examine whether FSNPs moved along with the ingested food, another experiment similar to the depuration described above was conducted by providing brine shrimp nauplii with DAPI-stained baker’s yeast as food and FSNPs simultaneously. The nauplii were then examined under a fluorescence microscope.

Chronic toxicity test Based on the results of the appropriate FSNP concentration experiment, a concentration of 16 mg/L FSNPs was used for the chronic toxicity test. Brine shrimp nauplii (18–24 h post-hatching) were transferred to 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 150 mL of artificial seawater under continuous aeration, with 10 nauplii per flask. They were fed with artificial food, and both seawater and food were renewed every 48 h. Three treatment groups were performed: (1) continuous exposure to FSNPs, (2) 3-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h, and (3) 6-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h. In treatments (2) and (3), nauplii were exposed to FSNPs prior to the renewal of seawater and food. The experiment was conducted over a period of 14 days. A control group was maintained in artificial seawater without FSNPs. Rearing conditions and mortality assessment criteria were consistent with those used in the acute toxicity test. Each treatment was conducted in nine replications.

Test with adult brine shrimp Adult brine shrimp, 25 males and 24 females, were used to evaluate whether FSNPs could be applied to developed stages. The sexes were determined by the presence of a clasping organ (male) and brood sac (female). The shrimp were randomly selected from an aquarium and transferred into 24-well plates filled with 2 mL of baker’s yeast suspension (1 × 10 6  cells/mL), one individual per well. They were dark-acclimatized for 30 min. The FSNP suspension was then added to each well to reach a final NP concentration of 16 mg/L. Observations were made every 5 min under UV light to detect the appearance of abdominal fluorescence, followed by further monitoring until luminescent feces were detected, indicating complete gut passage of the ingested FSNPs.

Statistical analyses Because our data did not meet the assumption for parametric statistics, nonparametric statistical analyses were used in all tests. The effects of FSNP concentration on mortality and immobility were ascertained by applying the Kruskal–Wallis test; Dunn’s test was used for pairwise comparison. The effects of FSNP concentration, the presence or absence of food, and their interaction with the marking efficiency or fluorescence brightness of the marked individuals were analyzed employing the aligned rank test. Feeding rates in the presence and absence of FSNPs were corrected for the rate of yeast autolysis in the control group and then compared by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The effects of depuration time, the presence or absence of food, and their interactions were analyzed using the aligned rank and Dunn’s tests. Locomotion data for shrimp treated with FSNPs were compared with the control utilizing the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The number of times that the abdomen of adult brine shrimp exhibited luminescence and the number of times that the fluorescent feces appeared due to the excretion of FSNPs were compared between sexes using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. LT 50  was analyzed using probit analysis in SPSS version 28.0 44 . All other statistical analyses were performed using the base, ARTool, combinate, dplyr, survival, survminer, and tidyverse packages in R, version 4.3.0 45 .
